# Pinning Packages with renv {#sec-dependencies}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*In order to exactly reproduce a given result, it may be
necessary to use programs in the exact versions used
originally.*

[Sandve, Nekrutenko, Taylor, and Hovig]{.smallcaps}, *Ten
Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research*,
Rule 3 (2013)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::



By the end of this chapter you will be able to pin the
exact version of every package an analysis uses. A
colleague who restores the lockfile a year from now will
then run the same code against the same packages as the
original run, rather than whatever happens to be current
on their machine. You will also be able to say precisely
which layer of the determinant stack that pin does and
does not reach.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 45 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder,
the determinant stack, and the capture-versus-validation
vocabulary this chapter relies on throughout.
@sec-compendium, for the `DESCRIPTION` file and the
R-package archetype the dependency triad draws its
middle term from. Statistically, nothing beyond reading
a package version number is required. R knowledge
assumed: calling `library()`, installing a package, and
reading a JSON file as a nested list; no prior exposure
to `renv` itself is assumed.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- Explain the package-churn failure mode, and say why
  pinning package versions is the step that lifts an
  analysis from locatable (L0) to package-pinned (L1)?
- Describe what an `renv.lock` file records, and carry
  out the init, snapshot, and restore workflow that
  produces and consumes it?
- State the dependency-triad invariant relating the
  code, the `DESCRIPTION`, and the lockfile, and run the
  automated check that keeps the three in agreement?
- Configure a dated snapshot of a package repository so
  that a restore draws fixed versions, as pre-compiled
  binaries where the platform is served?
- Delimit what `renv` does and does not pin, and thus
  explain why a lockfile alone cannot reach the
  pinned-environment level?

**Outline.** The package-churn failure mode and the
L0-to-L1 transition it motivates; the three judgments
that stay with the analyst; packrat to renv and what a
lockfile records; the init, snapshot, restore workflow;
the dependency-triad invariant and the automated check
that enforces it; dated snapshots of a package
repository; the limits of renv; lighter alternatives;
the cohort's own dependencies, scanned for real;
collaborating with an LLM; exercises, a cheat sheet, and
further reading.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: from earlier chapters

A colleague clones your cohort repository at its
submission tag and runs `analysis/scripts/01-clean.R` on
the unchanged raw extract. The cleaned table has fewer
rows than the committed
`analysis/data/derived_data/cohort_clean.csv`. The history
shows that the outlier threshold in the script was
tightened after that file was last committed. On the same
machine, the script as it stood when the file was
committed reproduces the file's row count. Drawing on
@sec-levels, @sec-version-control, and @sec-compendium,
name the failure and the rule it breaks.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The cleaned cohort table with fewer rows exposes a stale
derived file, not a package or environment change. On one
machine the old script reproduces the old count and the
current script does not, so only the analysis code
differs. The committed file breaks the promise of
@sec-compendium that a file in `derived_data/` can always
be regenerated from the raw inputs and the code. The
history of @sec-version-control locates the change:
`git log` on the script lists the commit, and `git show`
displays its diff. The tag secures L0 on the ladder of
@sec-levels. It fixes which code a reader finds, not that
a stored output still matches that code. The remedy is
to regenerate the file from the raw extract and the
current script.
:::
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

This chapter's whole business is the lockfile, so it is
the clearest capture in the book so far. It pins, for
the first time, the package-versions layer of the
determinant stack that @sec-levels laid out. That is
exactly the step from L0 to L1. @fig-stack-dependencies
marks that single layer against the ambient nine, with
every other layer left faded as secured, or left
unpinned, elsewhere.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Package versions'),
  title = 'Pinning packages captures one layer, and one layer only')
```

## Orientation

To illustrate, consider a familiar situation. A doctoral student
completes the analysis for a registry study of
hospital readmissions, renders a clean report, and
deposits the code alongside the manuscript. The work
is under version control, so a reader can locate every
script; on the ladder of @sec-levels the analysis has
reached L0, locatable. Eighteen months later a
reviewer asks for a minor revision. The student pulls
the repository onto a new laptop, installs the
packages afresh, and reruns the analysis. The model
now reports a different coefficient. Nothing in the
code changed. What changed is that `dplyr` had moved
from version 1.1.0 to 1.2.1, a grouping default had
been refined, and one intermediate summary was
computed over a slightly different partition.
The number in the published table can no
longer be regenerated, and the student cannot say with
certainty which number was correct.

This is the package-churn failure mode. It is the
specifically computational failure that the empirical
studies of @sec-crisis isolate. The R package
ecosystem is healthy precisely because it changes:
maintainers fix bugs, sharpen defaults, and deprecate
awkward interfaces. Every such improvement is,
however, a potential threat to the exact reproduction
of an analysis written against the older behavior. A
script names the packages it loads but almost never the
versions it loaded them at. It therefore inherits
whatever versions the next machine happens to provide.

The remedy for this one layer is a lockfile, a file that
records the exact version of every package the analysis
used so that the same set can be reinstalled later.
Recording that file is the transition from L0 to L1, from
locatable to package-pinned, and it is the whole business
of this chapter. We shall be equally careful about the
transition's limit. A lockfile pins the packages and
nothing beneath them. An analysis at L1 is therefore
pinned at the package layer and exposed at every layer
below, a boundary that motivates the container of
@sec-containers.

The chapter proceeds as follows. We begin with the three
judgments that stay with the analyst, then trace the line
from packrat to renv and examine what a lockfile records.
We next work through the init, snapshot, and restore
workflow, the dependency-triad invariant and the automated
check that enforces it, and dated snapshots of a package
repository. We then set out the limits of renv and some
lighter alternatives. Lastly, we scan the cohort's own
dependencies for real and consider how to collaborate
with an LLM on this material.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: naming the failure

The student's code did not change, and the published
table can no longer be regenerated. What single
determinant changed, and what artifact would have
prevented the drift?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The package-versions layer changed. `dplyr` moved from
1.1.0 to 1.2.1 between the original run and the
revision, and a refined grouping default altered an
intermediate summary. A committed `renv.lock`, restored
rather than freshly installed, would have reinstalled
the exact version the student originally ran against.
That would have closed the gap the bare script left open.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

The tooling in this chapter automates a great deal.
However, three judgments remain irreducibly the
analyst's.

1. **Deciding when to snapshot, and what a snapshot
   claims.** A lockfile is a dated assertion that these
   versions produced this result. The analyst chooses
   the moment to make that assertion, typically once an
   analysis is stable, and must understand that a
   snapshot taken mid-exploration pins whatever
   half-installed state the library happens to be in.

2. **Distinguishing a result dependency from a
   development tool.** No scanner can know that
   `languageserver` powers the editor while `dplyr`
   powers the analysis. The analyst must keep the
   lockfile an honest, minimal record of what
   determines the result, and keep mere tooling out of
   it, a distinction we develop below and that the
   accompanying whitepaper treats at length.

3. **Matching the reproducibility claim to the layer
   actually pinned.** A lockfile secures the package
   layer and no other. Presenting a lockfile-equipped
   analysis as fully reproducible, when the R version,
   the operating system, and the system libraries
   remain unpinned, overstates what has been achieved,
   and only the analyst can prevent that.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Lockfile.** A machine-generated file, `renv.lock`,
  recording the R version, the package repositories, and
  the exact version and source of every package the
  project uses, together with metadata copied from each
  package's `DESCRIPTION`.
- **Package library.** The directory into which R
  installs packages. A project-local library belongs to
  one project rather than being shared across all of a
  user's work.
- **Snapshot.** The act of scanning a project, resolving
  the versions currently installed, and writing them
  into the lockfile.
- **Restore.** The reverse act of reading the lockfile
  and reinstalling exactly the packages it records.
- **`DESCRIPTION`.** The human-authored file that
  declares a project's direct dependencies by role
  (`Imports`, `Suggests`, `Depends`), with optional
  version floors.
- **Package record.** The lockfile entry for one
  package: its name, version, and source, plus fields
  such as `Imports` and `License` copied from its
  `DESCRIPTION`. It contains no checksum of the package's
  files.
- **Package repository.** A server, such as CRAN or the
  Posit Package Manager, from which packages are
  installed.
- **Dated snapshot.** A view of a repository frozen as
  it stood on a particular calendar day, so that an
  install run today and one run next year fetch the same
  versions.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: tool versus judgment

`renv::snapshot()` can scan a project's code for packages
and write them to the lockfile automatically. Name one of
the three judgments above that this automation does not
make for the analyst.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Any one of the three. The first is the moment at which a
snapshot is taken, and therefore what state of the
library it asserts as correct. The second is the
distinction between a package the result depends on and a
package that merely serves the analyst's editor or
workflow. The third is the honest match between the
reproducibility claim made and the layer the lockfile
actually pins. The scan makes none of these three
decisions.
:::
:::

## From packrat to renv

We begin with some history. The idea of a project-local
library governed by a lockfile is not new to R. The `packrat` package,
begun in 2013 and on CRAN from 2014, was the first widely adopted
attempt to give each project its own isolated set of
packages recorded in a manifest. Its mechanics were
sound but its ergonomics were not, and it acquired a
reputation for surprising behavior that discouraged
routine use. The `renv` package, introduced by
@ushey2020 and now the community standard, superseded
it in 2019. It kept the essential idea, a project-local
library plus a lockfile. However, it rebuilt the surface
around a small, predictable set of verbs, a
human-readable JSON lockfile, and a shared package cache.
The cache lets many projects share one physical copy of a
given package version.

The design separates two things. The **library** is where
packages physically live; the **lockfile** is the
written record of what should live there. The two are
kept in agreement by two complementary operations. A
snapshot reads the library and updates the lockfile to
match it; a restore reads the lockfile and updates the
library to match it. Everything `renv` does is a
variation on keeping these two representations in step.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: library or lockfile

A teammate deletes their project's library folder by
accident, but the lockfile is untouched and committed.
Which operation restores their ability to work, and which
of the two representations was lost?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`renv::restore()` restores it, by reading the lockfile and
reinstalling the packages it records into a fresh library.
What was lost was the library, where packages physically
live. The lockfile, the written record of what should live
there, was never at risk, because it is a small committed
text file rather than a directory of installed code.
:::
:::

### What the lockfile records

The lockfile is the artifact that does the pinning, so
it repays close reading. The top of the file records the
R version and the repositories in force. Below that, each
package has a record giving its exact version and the
source it came from. Fields copied from the package's own
`DESCRIPTION` follow: its title, license, declared
dependencies, whether it contains compiled code, and more.
The excerpt below comes from a lockfile that `renv` 1.2.3
wrote on 2026-10-11, under R 4.6.1, for a one-line script
that calls `library(dplyr)`. It is shown as a static block
because `renv` does not run while this book renders. It is
abbreviated only by deleting fields and records; nothing
has been added or reordered.
The record for `dplyr` omits, among others, its `Type`,
`Authors@R`, `Description`, `URL`, and `Suggests`
fields.

```json
{
  "R": {
    "Version": "4.6.1",
    "Repositories": [
      {
        "Name": "CRAN",
        "URL": "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2026-06-29"
      }
    ]
  },
  "Packages": {
    "dplyr": {
      "Package": "dplyr",
      "Version": "1.2.1",
      "Source": "Repository",
      "Title": "A Grammar of Data Manipulation",
      "License": "MIT + file LICENSE",
      "Depends": [
        "R (>= 4.1.0)"
      ],
      "Imports": [
        "cli (>= 3.6.2)",
        "generics",
        "glue (>= 1.3.2)",
        "lifecycle (>= 1.0.5)",
        "magrittr (>= 1.5)",
        "methods",
        "pillar (>= 1.9.0)",
        "R6",
        "rlang (>= 1.1.7)",
        "tibble (>= 3.2.0)",
        "tidyselect (>= 1.2.0)",
        "utils",
        "vctrs (>= 0.7.1)"
      ],
      "NeedsCompilation": "yes",
      "Repository": "CRAN"
    }
  }
}
```

Four features deserve comment. First, the version is
recorded exactly, `1.2.1` and not `>= 1.2`, so there is
no latitude for a later install to drift upward. The
version floors inside `Imports`, such as
`rlang (>= 1.1.7)`, are a different thing. They are
`dplyr`'s own statement of what it tolerates, copied
from its `DESCRIPTION`. The pin for `rlang` is the exact
version in `rlang`'s own record.

Second, the source is named. A package that came from
CRAN, from a Posit Package Manager mirror, from
Bioconductor, or from a specific GitHub commit is
recorded as such. By default `renv::restore()` looks for
it in the same place, since the same version number can
denote different code on different repositories. The
`Repository` value is the registered name of the
repository the package was drawn from, matching one of
the names in the `Repositories` block above. This is why the excerpt records `CRAN` even
though that entry points at a Posit mirror.

Third, the closure is complete. Every contributed
package that `dplyr` needs, directly or through another
package, has a record of its own: the full file also
holds records for `rlang`, `vctrs`, `tibble`, and the
rest, and one for `renv` itself. Base packages such as
`methods` and `utils` come with R and have none.

Fourth, and easily misread, the record contains no
checksum of the package's files. Lockfiles written by
`renv` before version 1.1.0 carried a `Hash` field and a
`Requirements` list, and older tutorials still show
them. The change is recorded in the NEWS file that ships
with `renv`. That `Hash` was a fingerprint of selected
`DESCRIPTION` fields, which `renv` uses to key its
package cache. It was never a hash of the installed
files, so it could not confirm that a restored package
was byte-identical to the one recorded. A lockfile in
either format therefore cannot detect a repository that
serves altered contents under an unchanged version
string. That protection, such as it is, rests with the
repository.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A reader who has worked with `renv` before 1.1.0 may
look for the old `Hash` field and, finding it absent in
a current lockfile, worry that integrity checking has
been removed. Nothing has been lost, because the old
`Hash` never checked file integrity in the first place.
It only fingerprinted `DESCRIPTION` fields for the
package cache. The actual pitfall is believing either
format's record proves the installed bytes match what
was recorded. Neither does, and a lockfile's protection
against a repository silently serving different code
under the same version string is exactly nil.
:::

### The init, snapshot, restore workflow

Three commands drive the ordinary lifecycle. None of
them can execute while this book renders, so we show
them as static R blocks. The reader runs them at an
interactive prompt inside the project.

Initialization creates the project-local library and a
first lockfile.

```r
renv::init()
```

From this point, packages installed into the project go
into its private library rather than the shared
system-wide one. One project's `dplyr` upgrade
therefore cannot disturb another's. As the analysis develops and
new packages are installed, a snapshot writes the
current state into the lockfile.

```r
renv::snapshot()
```

The snapshot does not blindly record every installed
package. It first scans the project's source for the
packages the code actually references, through
`library()`, `require()`, and `pkg::fun()` calls, and
records those together with their transitive
dependencies. A package sitting in the library but
called nowhere in the code is, by default, left out.

On another machine, or the same machine a year later, a
restore reads the lockfile and rebuilds the library to
match.

```r
renv::restore()
```

A collaborator who clones the repository and calls
`renv::restore()` obtains the exact package set the
analysis was written against, irrespective of what
versions are current.

In the framework this book uses, this lifecycle is
partly automated so that an analyst does not forget the
snapshot. The project's generated `.Rprofile` installs
an exit hook that snapshots the library when an
interactive session ends, and restores missing packages
when a session begins. A package installed during
analysis is thus captured. The automation removes the
two most common ways the library and the lockfile drift
apart.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

To see the pin actually hold: note the installed version
of one package (`packageVersion('dplyr')`), delete the
project library, run `renv::restore()`, and confirm the
same version comes back. To make it fail on purpose,
open `renv.lock` in a text editor, change one package's
`Version` field to a release that does not exist, and
rerun `renv::restore()`. It reports that the requested
version cannot be found, rather than silently installing
something else.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: snapshot versus restore

A colleague clones your project, opens R, and is
puzzled that the packages are not yet installed. They
ask whether they should run `renv::snapshot()` to get
them. What do you advise, and why?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

They should run `renv::restore()`, not
`renv::snapshot()`. Restore reads the existing lockfile
and installs the recorded versions into the local
library, which is exactly what a fresh clone needs.
Snapshot runs in the opposite direction. It would
overwrite the lockfile with whatever is currently
installed, which on a fresh clone is nothing relevant.
It would thereby destroy the very record the colleague
needs. The mnemonic is that snapshot writes the
lockfile and restore reads it.
:::
:::

## The dependency-triad invariant

A lockfile solves the pinning problem. However, it
introduces a bookkeeping problem in its place: the
lockfile can fall out of step with the code it is
supposed to describe. A contributor installs a package
for an exploratory notebook and forgets to snapshot, so
the code now uses a package the lockfile does not
record. Or a package is dropped from the analysis but
left in the project's `DESCRIPTION`, so the declared
dependencies name something the code no longer touches.
Either drift silently degrades the pin.

But how are we to know that the lockfile still describes
the code? The framework this book uses formalizes the correct
relationship as the dependency triad. Three sources of
information describe the packages an analysis uses, and
in a healthy compendium they satisfy a nesting relation.

- The **code** references some set of packages, through
  its `library()`, `require()`, and `pkg::fun()` calls.
- The **`DESCRIPTION`** declares a set of direct
  dependencies.
- The **`renv.lock`** records a set of pinned packages.

The invariant is the composition of two atomic
inclusions, each set contained in the next:

$$
\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{DESCRIPTION}
\subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}.
$$

Read left to right, it says that every package the code
calls must be declared in `DESCRIPTION`, and every
declared dependency must be pinned in the lockfile. The
lockfile is the largest set because it also records the
transitive dependencies that the analyst never named
directly. Base packages, which every R installation
provides at the R version's own version, are excluded
from the code set. Recommended packages such as
`survival` also ship with R, but they are versioned
independently of it and `renv` records them in the
lockfile, so they stay in. The first inclusion therefore
concerns every package that is not base.

The invariant needs one qualification. Its strict
form, with `DESCRIPTION` as the binding middle term,
holds cleanly for the R-package archetype. There
`DESCRIPTION` is the package's declared dependency
interface, and every package the code calls belongs there
by definition. For a research or analysis compendium the
middle term is looser. In that case `DESCRIPTION`
declares only the API of the reusable code in `R/`, while
packages used solely by analysis scripts or reports
legitimately live in `renv.lock` without appearing in
`DESCRIPTION`. The operative invariant for a compendium is
therefore the weaker $\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$.
That is, the strict `DESCRIPTION` inclusion is exact for
the package archetype but archetype-conditional in
general. As a matter of placement an analysis-script
dependency may still be listed in `DESCRIPTION` under
`Suggests`. However, the framework does not enforce the
strict `DESCRIPTION` inclusion as a gate on a compendium,
precisely because that inclusion does not hold for one.
The gate it enforces
on a compendium is the single inclusion $\mathrm{Code}
\subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$, that nothing the code uses
goes unpinned. The strict double inclusion is applied only
in the package archetype, where `DESCRIPTION` is the
authoritative dependency interface.

@fig-triad draws the nesting, with the archetype
qualification marked. A package may sit legitimately in
any of the three bands; the only broken position is
outside the lockfile altogether.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

bands <- tibble(
  label = c('renv.lock: everything pinned',
            'DESCRIPTION: declared',
            'Code: actually called'),
  xmin = c(0.4, 1.5, 2.5), xmax = c(9.6, 8.5, 7.5),
  ymin = c(0.5, 1.3, 2.1), ymax = c(6.2, 5.4, 4.6),
  fill = c('#eef4f4', '#dcebea', '#c3ddda')
)

items <- tibble(
  x = c(5.0, 5.0, 2.6, 7.4),
  y = c(3.3, 1.75, 0.92, 0.92),
  lab = c('dplyr\n(called, declared, pinned)',
          'an unused declaration',
          'rlang, vctrs\n(transitive)',
          'ggplot2, used only by\nanalysis scripts')
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = bands,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax,
                ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = fill),
            color = 'grey40', linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_text(data = bands, aes(x = xmin + 0.15, y = ymax - 0.25,
                              label = label),
            hjust = 0, fontface = 'bold', size = 3.1) +
  geom_text(data = items, aes(x = x, y = y, label = lab),
            size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.95, color = 'grey20') +
  annotate('point', x = 3.55, y = 0.02, shape = 4,
           size = 2.6, stroke = 1.1, color = '#a33') +
  annotate('text', x = 3.75, y = 0.02, hjust = 0,
           label = 'survival: used but unpinned',
           size = 3.1, fontface = 'bold', color = '#a33') +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.2, 9.8), ylim = c(-0.35, 6.4)) +
  theme_void()
```

The invariant can be checked by machine. The framework's
`check-renv` gate, backed by
the `zzrenvcheck` package, scans all three sources and
tests the two inclusions. It reports any violation: a
package used in code but undeclared, or declared but
unpinned. It can also repair a violation on request. It
writes a missing declaration into `DESCRIPTION` through
the `desc` package. For a package absent from the
lockfile, it writes a record of the version installed in
the analyst's library, the version the code was actually
run against. Only when the package is not installed at
all does it fall back to the current CRAN version. It
then prints a warning saying so, since that version may
not be the one that produced any result. The repair does
not call `renv::snapshot()` or `install.packages()`; it
edits the two manifests as text. Two limits follow.
First, the record it writes is minimal, a name, version,
and source without the copied `DESCRIPTION` metadata.
Second, it covers the missing package alone, not that
package's own dependencies. The repair is therefore a prompt to
review, and a later `renv::snapshot()` remains the
authoritative record of the library.

```bash
$ make check-renv
```

In the framework this book uses, this target runs the
check with repair enabled before a commit. Outside the
framework the same call is
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE)`. Under
continuous integration the check must run with repair
disabled and must be able to fail the build:

```bash
Rscript -e "zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = FALSE, strict = TRUE, error_on_fail = TRUE)"
```

When `error_on_fail` is true, a failed check stops with
an error and `Rscript` exits with a nonzero status. That
is what turns the job red. Current `zzrenvcheck` already
defaults to `error_on_fail = !interactive()`, so a script
or CI job fails while an interactive console only
reports. Nevertheless, the CI call above passes the
argument explicitly so that the gate does not depend on
how R was started. We confirmed the failure on a scratch project
whose code called `dplyr` without declaring it: the
command above printed 'Validation failed' and exited
with status 1. `zzrenvcheck` is not on CRAN, so the CI
job installs it first. The gate tool is itself a
dependency of the evidence it produces, so the job pins
it to one commit rather than to whatever the default
branch holds on the day of the run:

```r
remotes::install_github(
  'rgt47/zzrenvcheck@6f53235668cb4048c1ae793d64b10d6505bf69a2'
)
```

That commit is `zzrenvcheck` 0.10.0, the version whose
behavior this section describes. A drift
that escaped the developer's machine therefore fails the
build rather than being silently repaired. This forces
the contributor to commit the fix instead of letting the
clean build paper over it. The gate is a presence check.
That is, it guarantees that the three sets nest, that
nothing used is unpinned. It does not
verify that the version floors in `DESCRIPTION` agree
with the exact pins in the lockfile, which is a separate
concern.

The gate is also archetype-aware. When it finds an
`analysis/` directory at the project root it enters
compendium mode automatically (`compendium = "auto"` is
the default). In that mode only packages used in `R/` are
required in `DESCRIPTION`, while packages used only in
`analysis/` or `scripts/` need only appear in
`renv.lock`. On an R-package project, which has no
`analysis/` directory, the strict double inclusion
applies. Passing `compendium = TRUE` or
`compendium = FALSE` overrides the auto-detection when
the directory layout does not reflect the archetype.

### Scanning the documentation, not only the code

The most common way for a dependency check to fail is
subtle. It scans the analysis code, pronounces the
project consistent, and overlooks a package that is used
only in a vignette or in the rendered manuscript. That is
exactly where a documentation build breaks on a fresh
machine. `zzrenvcheck` deliberately scans more widely
than a plain code scan on this point.

The scan does not look at `.R` scripts alone. It parses
the literate and dynamic documents as well, R Markdown
(`.Rmd`), Quarto (`.qmd`), and Sweave (`.Rnw`). A package
loaded inside a report chunk or a vignette is thus seen
just as one loaded in `R/` is. Within every such file it
recognizes each of the forms by which R code reaches for a
package. These are the explicit `library(pkg)` and
`require(pkg)`, the namespaced `pkg::function()`, and the
roxygen2 directives `@import` and `@importFrom` from which
a package's `.Rd` help files are generated. In its strict
mode it widens the search beyond the analysis
directories, into the `tests/`, `vignettes/`, and `inst/`
directories. It is correspondingly careful about what it
ignores. `README` files and the example directories
(`man/examples`, `inst/examples`) are skipped, since the
install-and-demonstrate code they usually carry would
otherwise raise false alarms. A separate pass reads the
reproducibility files themselves, the `Dockerfile`, the
`Makefile`, `install.sh`, and `.Rprofile`, for
version-pinned installs such as `pak('survival@3.5-8')`.
This pass catches a version fixed in the container recipe
that has drifted from the lockfile.

Consider a manuscript compendium whose analysis in `R/`
restores cleanly from the lockfile. Its report, however,
draws a forest plot with a plotting package that appears
nowhere except the `.qmd` itself. A scanner that read only
the code would certify the project as consistent. The
report would then fail to render on the reviewer's machine
for want of an unpinned package. Because `zzrenvcheck`
reads the document, the missing dependency is caught and
pinned before it can break the build. The wider reach
helps most with the scholarly manuscript and the blog,
whose rendered outputs are the deliverable. Their package
needs sit in documents, where a naive check does not look.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what a code-only scan misses

A manuscript's `R/` directory restores cleanly from the
lockfile, but its `.qmd` report loads a plotting package
nowhere referenced in `R/`. Would a dependency check that
scans only `.R` files catch the missing pin, and why does
`zzrenvcheck` catch it where that scan would not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. A code-only scan sees only `R/`, finds every package
it references already pinned, and certifies the project
consistent while the report's own dependency goes unseen.
`zzrenvcheck` catches it because it also parses literate
documents, `.Rmd` and `.qmd` among them, for `library()`,
`require()`, and `pkg::fun()` calls. A package loaded
only inside a report chunk is therefore scanned exactly
as one loaded in `R/` would be.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice, the `check-renv` gate and the
lockfile it enforces, reaches L1 package-pinned and
nothing further. It leaves the R version, the operating
system, and the system libraries beneath the package layer
entirely exposed.
:::

### The triad across archetypes

The lockfile discipline is identical across the
archetypes of @sec-compendium, because every archetype
records its packages in the same `renv.lock` by the
same snapshot and restore. What varies slightly is how
natural the declared-dependency middle term feels. In
the R-package archetype, `DESCRIPTION` is the package's
defining interface:
`R CMD check` reads it, an installer reads it, and CRAN
reads it. The triad is therefore especially natural
there, since the declared set already exists for
reasons independent of reproducibility. A data-analysis
project, a manuscript compendium, a simulation study,
and a blog also carry a `DESCRIPTION`. There, however, it
declares only the API of the reusable code in `R/`.
Their binding invariant is instead the single
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$. The
`check-renv` gate applies that weaker rule automatically
when it detects an `analysis/` directory. A subtlety
follows for the R-package archetype. A package used only
by an analysis script or report belongs in `Suggests`
rather than `Imports`. In that way `R CMD check` does not
hard-require a package the package's own exported
functions never call.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: locating a drift

Continuous integration on an R-package archetype fails
with the message that `survival` is used in `R/model.R`
but is not declared in `DESCRIPTION`. Which inclusion of
the triad has been violated, and what single command
would most likely repair it?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The invariant is the composition of two atomic
inclusions. The one violated here is the first,
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{DESCRIPTION}$: the code
references `survival` while `DESCRIPTION` does not
declare it. This in turn leaves it unpinned in the
lockfile. The transitive composition
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$ therefore
fails as a consequence, but the atomic breach is at the
code-to-`DESCRIPTION` step. The likely cause is that
`survival` was installed interactively but never
declared. Running `make check-renv`, which invokes
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages()` with automatic repair,
would write `survival` into `DESCRIPTION` through the
`desc` package. It would also add a record of the
installed `survival` version to `renv.lock`, restoring
both inclusions. This edits the two manifests as text and is distinct
from an `renv::snapshot()`, which would instead re-derive
the lockfile from the installed library. The fix must
then be committed so the clean CI build sees it.
:::
:::

## Dated snapshots of a package repository

A lockfile records which versions to install. But a
plain CRAN mirror will happily serve only whatever is
current. Moreover, older source packages must often be
recompiled, which is slow and can fail when a system
library has since moved on. The Posit Package Manager
resolves both problems by offering dated snapshots of
CRAN. A snapshot URL freezes the repository as it stood
on one calendar day. A request for a package then
returns the version that was current on that date, and,
on a platform the manager serves, returns it as a
pre-compiled binary rather than as source to be built.
On Linux that requires the URL form described below.

The mechanism is a URL that embeds a date.

```r
options(repos = c(
  CRAN = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2026-06-29"
))
```

With repositories pointed at a dated snapshot, an
install run today and the same install run next year
draw from an identical, frozen catalog. The
lockfile above records exactly this URL in its
`Repositories` block, so that a restore reproduces both
the versions and the source they came from. The gain is
twofold. The first gain is fixity, because the catalog
cannot drift, and the second is speed, because binaries
install in seconds where source builds take minutes. On
Linux the binary path is more specific. Pre-compiled
binaries are served from a distribution-specific form of
the URL, such as
`https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/__linux__/noble/2026-06-29`,
and R may need to send its version in the HTTP user agent.
The plain dated path shown above should be expected to
deliver source to be built. In the framework this book uses, the
project's generated configuration points R at a dated
snapshot automatically. The two benefits thus accrue
without the analyst assembling the URL by hand. The date
of the snapshot becomes, in effect, part of the
environment's identity. We take up this topic again when
the container fixes a snapshot date at image-build time
in @sec-containers.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: fixity versus speed

A colleague points their `repos` option at
`https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/2026-06-29` and
reports that installs are both faster and identical a
year later. Are these the same benefit or two different
ones, and what does each depend on?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Two different benefits. The speed comes from the
snapshot serving a pre-compiled binary rather than
source to be built. It depends on the platform-specific
binary path being used (the distribution-codename form on
Linux) and on a binary existing for that platform. The
identical-a-year-later fixity comes from the date
embedded in the URL freezing the catalog. It holds
regardless of whether a binary or a source install is
served. A snapshot with no binaries for a given
platform still delivers the fixity without the speed.
:::
:::

## The limits of renv

A lockfile is easy to overclaim, and the gap it leaves
is the subject of the next chapter. But what, exactly,
does a lockfile leave unpinned? `renv` pins the R
packages. It does not pin the R interpreter itself, so a
lockfile produced under R 4.6.0 may restore under R 4.2.1
with different results. It may also fail to restore at
all when a recorded version requires a newer R. It does
not pin the operating
system, so a lockfile assembled on macOS carries no
guarantee on Linux. And it does not pin the system
libraries that many packages link against, the GDAL
behind a spatial package or the `libxml2` behind an XML
parser. A restore on a machine lacking a required
system library may therefore fail to compile a package
or, more insidiously, may install a differently
behaving one.

`renv` does its one job well, but the package layer is
one layer of a taller stack. Pinning it leaves every
layer beneath it as the next machine happens to provide.
@ushey2020 designed `renv` to solve the package problem
and no more; the environment problem is out of its scope
by design. An analysis equipped with a faithful lockfile
has reached L1, pinned packages, and every layer beneath
the packages remains exposed. Closing that remaining gap is the work of the
container, and it is where @sec-containers begins.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what a lockfile cannot promise

A lockfile produced under R 4.6.0 is restored on a
colleague's machine running R 4.2.1, and the restore
succeeds without error. Does this mean the analysis will
produce the same result on both machines?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Not necessarily. `renv` pins the package versions, not the
R interpreter itself. A successful restore under a
different R version means the packages installed, not that
they behave identically under that R. The lockfile's `R`
block records which R version wrote it, but it neither
installs nor enforces that version. When the project
loads under a different minor release of R, `renv` prints
a one-line notice naming both versions, and then proceeds
under the R it was given. Closing this
exposure is the work of the container in @sec-containers,
which pins the R runtime along with the packages.
:::
:::

## Lighter and alternative approaches

The lockfile-and-restore idiom is not the only way to
pin the package layer. The reader should know the
principal alternatives, because some suit particular
settings better and because the tradeoffs illuminate
what `renv` is doing.

The most important shift of idiom is from preserving a
lockfile to reconstructing an environment from a date.
The `rang` package of @chan2023 takes a set of packages
and a target date, and resolves the versions that were
current then. It reaches back through CRAN's archive to
reconstruct a historical environment, even for a project
that never recorded a lockfile at all. Where `renv`
requires foresight, a committed lockfile written while
the analysis was live, `rang` offers hindsight,
recovering an approximate environment after the fact.
It is the natural instrument for a legacy analysis that
one wishes to resurrect.

The `groundhog` package of @simonsohn2026 pursues the
same date-based idea but at a different point in the
workflow. Rather than restoring a library before the
script runs, it loads version-specific packages at run
time. A `groundhog.library()` call carries a date, and
the packages current on that date are loaded for that
session. It needs no project library and no snapshot
step. In effect, it trades `renv`'s explicit committed
lockfile for a date-stamped call evaluated against the
repository's history. The cost of that convenience is
that the pin now lives inside the script's control flow
rather than in a separate, inspectable manifest. A
reviewer must read the code to discover it.

Finally, `capsule` [@capsule] is best understood as a
lazier discipline layered over `renv` itself. It defers
building the project library until it is actually needed.
The analyst develops against their ordinary user library
and materializes the pinned library only when
reproducing or checking the work. For analysts who
find `renv`'s always-on project library intrusive during
exploratory work, it lowers the friction of adoption
while preserving the lockfile as the eventual source of
truth.

Each of these approaches pins the package layer and only
the package layer. Whether the pin is a committed
lockfile, a reconstructed date, or a run-time call, none
reaches down to the R version, the operating system, or
the system libraries.
The choice among them is a choice of ergonomics and of
foresight versus hindsight, not a choice of how far down
the determinant stack one has pinned.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: foresight or hindsight

A legacy analysis from four years ago never recorded a
lockfile. Which of the three alternatives is suited to
recovering an approximate environment for it now, and
which two require the discipline to have been in place
from the start?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`rang` is suited to the legacy case, because it
reconstructs a past environment from a target date
through CRAN's archive, needing no prior lockfile at all.
`groundhog` and `capsule` both require the discipline in
place beforehand. `groundhog` needs the date-stamped
`groundhog.library()` call written into the script at the
time. `capsule` still layers over `renv`'s own snapshot,
so without one there is nothing for it to materialize
later.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the package-churn failure mode concrete, and to
generate a computed artifact at build time, we
construct a small synthetic lockfile diff. That is, we
compare two snapshots of the same project taken some
months apart. This is the kind of table a version-control
diff of `renv.lock` would summarize. Reading it is the
routine skill of noticing which pins moved. The data
are synthetic and no packages are installed; the
computation uses only `tibble`, `dplyr`, and `knitr`.


::: {#tbl-lockdiff .cell tbl-cap='A synthetic lockfile diff between two snapshots of one project. The changed column flags every package whose pinned version moved between the earlier and later snapshot.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

lock_diff <- tibble(
  package    = c('dplyr', 'ggplot2', 'tidyr',
                 'survival', 'lubridate', 'rlang'),
  version_a  = c('1.1.0', '3.4.4', '1.3.0',
                 '3.5-7', '1.9.3', '1.1.2'),
  version_b  = c('1.2.1', '3.4.4', '1.3.1',
                 '3.5-8', '1.9.3', '1.1.4')
) |>
  mutate(changed = if_else(
    version_a == version_b, '', 'changed'
  ))

knitr::kable(lock_diff)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|package   |version_a |version_b |changed |
|:---------|:---------|:---------|:-------|
|dplyr     |1.1.0     |1.2.1     |changed |
|ggplot2   |3.4.4     |3.4.4     |        |
|tidyr     |1.3.0     |1.3.1     |changed |
|survival  |3.5-7     |3.5-8     |changed |
|lubridate |1.9.3     |1.9.3     |        |
|rlang     |1.1.2     |1.1.4     |changed |


:::
:::


Between the two snapshots,
4 of the
6 pins moved. Three of the moves are patch-level (`tidyr`, `survival`,
and `rlang`), the kind that ordinarily preserve
behavior but occasionally do not. One is a minor
version bump (`dplyr`, from 1.1.0 to 1.2.1) of the sort
that can refine a default. The `rlang` move, from 1.1.2
to 1.1.4, deserves attention despite its size because of
its transitive position. Almost nothing calls `rlang`
directly, yet almost everything depends on it, so the
move happened beneath the whole stack. A diff of the
lockfile is a reviewable record of this churn. Without a
committed lockfile, none of these movements would be
visible, and the analyst confronted with a changed result
would have no way to see which package had shifted. The
lockfile cannot stop packages from changing, but it makes
the change legible and lets the analyst restore the
earlier column deliberately.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: reading the diff

In @tbl-lockdiff, `ggplot2`'s version is identical in
both snapshots and `rlang`'s moved by only a patch
release, yet the chapter singles out `rlang`'s move as
the more consequential one to notice. Why?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because consequence tracks transitive position, not the
size of the version jump. `rlang` sits beneath almost
every other package in the tidyverse closure. A change to
its behavior therefore propagates upward into everything
that depends on it, even though almost nothing in the
project's own code calls `rlang` directly. A patch-level move in a
package most analysts have never heard of can matter more
than a minor-version move in a package they call by name
every day.
:::
:::

## The cohort's own dependencies

In this section we apply the chapter's method to the
running cohort compendium. `renv::dependencies()` scans a
file for the packages its code actually references and
returns one row per package found. That is exactly the
scan `renv::snapshot()` runs before writing a lockfile.


::: {#tbl-cohort-deps .cell tbl-cap='Packages `renv::dependencies()` finds referenced in the two files that produce the running cohort, scanned directly rather than asserted. `simulate_cohort.R` contributes no rows because it calls base R functions (`rnorm`, `sample`, `as.Date`) without `library()` or a `::` prefix, so the scan finds no package name to report.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
deps <- renv::dependencies(
  c('../../R/cohort.R',
    '../../analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R')
)
#> Finding R package dependencies ... Done!
deps_tbl <- unique(deps[, c('Source', 'Package')])
deps_tbl$Source <- basename(deps_tbl$Source)
found_pkgs <- sort(unique(deps$Package))
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))
found_base <- intersect(found_pkgs, base_pkgs)
contributed <- setdiff(found_pkgs, base_pkgs)
has_lockfile <- file.exists('../../renv.lock')
lock_pkgs <- if (has_lockfile) {
  names(renv::lockfile_read('../../renv.lock')$Packages)
} else {
  character(0)
}
unpinned <- setdiff(contributed, lock_pkgs)
knitr::kable(deps_tbl, row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Source   |Package  |
|:--------|:--------|
|cohort.R |parallel |
|cohort.R |stats    |
|cohort.R |survival |
|cohort.R |tibble   |
|cohort.R |utils    |
|cohort.R |withr    |


:::
:::


`R/cohort.R` references
`parallel`, `stats`, `survival`, `tibble`, `utils`, and `withr`.
Of these, `parallel`, `stats`, and `utils`
are base packages: they ship with every R installation,
their version is the R version's, and a lockfile records
no entry for them. The counting rule for the rest is
whether `renv` records the package in the lockfile. A
recommended package such as `survival` also ships with
the standard R binaries, but it is versioned and updated
independently of R, so `renv` pins it like any other, and
we count it as contributed. Under that rule the scan finds
3 contributed packages,
`survival`, `tibble`, and `withr`.
The code is locatable and its dependencies are *known*,
from a real scan rather than from memory. Whether they are
also pinned is a question for the lockfile.
`file.exists('renv.lock')` at the project root is
TRUE, and of the contributed packages the
scan finds, the lockfile leaves 0
unrecorded. The package-versions layer is therefore
pinned, and the cohort compendium has reached at least L1.
For a compendium without a lockfile, `renv::init()`,
which scans the code and writes the first lockfile, and a
commit of that lockfile, is the single step that lifts it from
L0 to L1, exactly as the orientation above describes for
the hypothetical registry study.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why no rows for the simulator

`renv::dependencies()` returns no row for
`analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R`, even though that
script is essential to the cohort and uses functions such
as `rnorm()` and `sample()`. Is this a bug in the scan?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. `rnorm()` lives in the `stats` package and `sample()`
in the `base` package. Both, like `utils`, are base
packages bundled with every R installation rather than
contributed packages a lockfile needs to pin. The scan is
working as intended. It reports the packages a file names,
through `library()`, `require()`, or `pkg::`, and this
script names none. A base package named that way would
appear, as `stats` and `utils` do for `R/cohort.R`, but
the lockfile would still record no entry for it.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for the
mechanics of `renv`. However, a fluent, plausible-looking
lockfile instruction can pin the wrong thing or nothing
at all. Each of the following triples pairs a useful
prompt with what the analyst must watch for and verify.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data through
prompts with public generative AI tools, which it glosses as
third-party tools, as a breach of the data use certification.
It treats a model trained on such data as a data derivative,
to be shared only with other approved users and not kept
after the project closes [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts, so confine it to a branch and keep merges,
pushes, and deposits for yourself (@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


Dependency questions rarely need data at all.

**Prompt.** 'My collaborator cloned our project and the
packages are missing. Write the R command they should
run.'

*Watch for.* Check for advice to reinstall packages by
hand with `install.packages()`, or to run
`renv::snapshot()`, either of which is wrong for a fresh
clone. The correct answer is `renv::restore()`.

*Verification.* Confirm that the suggested command reads
the lockfile rather than writing it, and that after
running it the installed versions match the lockfile.
Run the check gate and confirm the triad holds.

With a coding agent the suggestion becomes an action.
An agent that runs `renv::snapshot()` in a fresh clone
can overwrite the lockfile with the state of whatever
library it finds there. Treat `renv.lock` as a protected
path: read its diff line by line before any commit that
touches it, and keep the decision to change it with the
analyst (@sec-llm-delegate).

**Prompt.** 'Explain why my `renv.lock` includes
`roxygen2` and `tinytest` when my analysis never calls
them, and whether I should remove them.'

*Watch for.* Check for a flat assertion that any unused
package should be purged, which misses the deliberate
convention by which test infrastructure is pinned while
pure development tooling is not. The distinction is a
judgment, not a rule the model can read off the file.

*Verification.* Decide the placement yourself against
the two-test procedure: does the package's version
affect the result, and does the code reference it?
Confirm that development-only tools such as
`languageserver` are in the Dockerfile and absent from
the lockfile, and that test packages are handled by your
stated convention.

**Prompt.** 'Set my repository to a dated Posit Package
Manager snapshot for 2026-06-29.'

*Watch for.* Check the URL for the wrong path
structure, an implausible date, or a mirror that does
not offer binaries for the analyst's platform. Check
also for a Linux distribution codename assumed without
comment that does not match the analyst's system.

*Verification.* Check the constructed URL against the
Posit Package Manager documentation, confirm the date is
the one you intend, and confirm that an install actually
draws binaries rather than falling back to source. The
recorded URL should then appear in the lockfile's
`Repositories` block.

*A better prompt.* 'My analysis runs on Ubuntu 24.04
(codename `noble`) with the R version recorded in the
attached `renv.lock`. Write the `options(repos = ...)`
call that points at the Posit Package Manager CRAN
snapshot dated 2026-06-29, in the form that serves Linux
binaries for that codename. Change no package version.
Tell me how to confirm that an install draws a binary
rather than building from source.'

## Exercises

1. Initialize `renv` in a throwaway project, install two
   packages, and snapshot. Open `renv.lock` in a text
   editor and locate, for one package, its `Version`, its
   `Source` and `Repository`, and its `Imports`. Explain
   in a sentence what each tells a later restore, and
   name one thing the record does not let a restore
   check. Report the `renv` version you used, since the
   lockfile format changed in `renv` 1.1.0.

2. With the project of Exercise 1, upgrade one package
   to a newer version, snapshot again, and inspect the
   diff of `renv.lock` under version control. Which
   fields changed, and which stayed fixed? Relate the
   diff to the synthetic table of @tbl-lockdiff.

3. Deliberately break the dependency triad: add a
   `library()` call for a package you have not declared
   or pinned. Run the project's dependency check and
   record which inclusion it reports as violated and how
   it repairs the violation. Then remove the call and
   confirm the check passes.

4. Point your repository at a dated Posit Package Manager
   snapshot and reinstall one package. Time the install,
   then compare it with an install of the same package
   from source. Report the difference and explain, in
   terms of binaries versus source, why it arises.

5. Take a small analysis that has no lockfile and use
   `rang` to reconstruct the package environment as it
   stood on a chosen past date. Compare the resulting
   version set with what a current `install.packages()`
   would provide. Which packages differ, and by how much?

6. Argue, in a short paragraph, why an analysis that
   passes its dependency check has reached L1 and not
   L2. Name one concrete determinant that a lockfile
   leaves unpinned and describe a plausible way it could
   change a result across two machines.

7. Run `renv::dependencies()` on `R/cohort.R` and
   `analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R` from the running
   cohort compendium, as @tbl-cohort-deps does. Report
   the number of distinct contributed (non-base) packages
   the scan finds and name them, counting a recommended
   package such as `survival` as contributed because
   `renv` pins it, and treating a package as base when
   `installed.packages(priority = 'base')` lists it. Then
   explain, from the scan alone and without reading
   `simulate_cohort.R`, why that file is permitted to
   contribute zero rows.

8. This exercise returns to the version-control chapter's
   discipline of distinguishing what must be committed
   from what must never be. `renv::init()` writes an
   `renv/` directory containing `activate.R`, a
   `settings.json`, and (once packages are installed) a
   `library/` subdirectory holding the actual installed

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Two of
the eight have no single correct answer, because what

## Exercise 1

The answer below assumes `renv` 1.1.0 or later. With
`renv` 1.2.3, the version used for this chapter, a
snapshot writes records in the format excerpted in the
chapter. The fields answer different questions a later
restore has to settle.

The **version** is recorded exactly, `1.2.1` and not
`>= 1.2`, so a restore installs the release the analysis
actually used and has no latitude to drift upward. This
is the field that defends against the ordinary failure,
in which a package acquires a new default between the
original run and the rerun.

The **source** names where the package came from: CRAN, a
Posit Package Manager mirror, Bioconductor, or a specific
GitHub commit. It matters because the same version number
can denote different code on different repositories, so
the version alone does not identify the package. Note
that the `Repository` value is the registered name of the
repository rather than its URL. That is why a lockfile
can record `CRAN` while the corresponding entry in the
`Repositories` block points at a Posit mirror.

The **`Imports`** list is copied from the package's own
`DESCRIPTION`. It tells a reader which other packages
this one needs, with the version floors its authors
declared, such as `rlang (>= 1.1.7)`. It is not itself a
pin: each of those dependencies is pinned by the exact
`Version` in its own record elsewhere in the file.

What the record does not let a restore check is whether
the files it installs are the files that were installed
before. There is no checksum of the package contents. A
reader working from an older tutorial may expect a
`Hash` field. `renv` before 1.1.0 wrote one, but it was a
fingerprint of `DESCRIPTION` fields used to key the
package cache, never a hash of the installed files.
Current `renv` does not write it.

A useful way to hold the fields together: the version
says which release, the source says whose copy of it,
and the copied metadata says what that release declared
about itself. None of them says whether the bytes match.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

For the upgraded package, `Version` changes, and so does
any field copied from `DESCRIPTION` that the new release
altered: commonly `Imports` and its version floors, the
`RoxygenNote`, and the author or maintainer fields. A
diff of one upgrade can therefore show many changed
lines for a single moved pin. The line to look for first
is `Version`. `Package`, `Source`, and
`Repository` stay fixed, since the package is the same
package drawn from the same place. A reader whose
lockfile shows a `Hash` field moving alongside the
version is running `renv` older than 1.1.0, which wrote
the older format.

Two further effects in the diff are easy to miss on a
first reading. If the upgraded package gained a
dependency, new package entries appear in the lockfile
that the reader never installed by name. This is because
the lockfile captures the full transitive closure rather
than the packages the reader asked for. And the `R` block
at the top of the file is untouched. It records the R
version under which the snapshot ran, but it does not
install or enforce that version (Exercise 6), and
upgrading a package does not change it.

The relation to @tbl-lockdiff is that the table shows the
same structure in synthetic form. Each row is a package,
the earlier and later columns hold the pinned versions,
and the flag marks where they differ. A real
`git diff renv.lock` is that table expressed as JSON, with
the additional detail that the copied `DESCRIPTION`
metadata moves with the version.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

The violated inclusion is the first atomic one,
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{DESCRIPTION}$. The code
now references a package that `DESCRIPTION` does not
declare. This in turn leaves it unpinned in the
lockfile, so the transitive composition
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$ fails as a
consequence. The breach to report is the atomic one, not
the consequence.

Running `make check-renv` invokes
`zzrenvcheck::check_packages()` with automatic repair. It
writes the package into `DESCRIPTION` through the `desc`
package and adds a record of its installed version to
`renv.lock`, restoring both inclusions. If the package is
not installed, the repair records the current CRAN
version instead and warns that it has done so. The
honest response to that warning is to install the
package, rerun the analysis, and repair again. This edits
the two manifests as text and is deliberately distinct
from an `renv::snapshot()`, which would instead re-derive
the whole lockfile from whatever is currently installed.

Removing the `library()` call and re-running the check
does make the check pass. However, it does not return the
manifests to their prior state: the repair already wrote
the package into `DESCRIPTION` and the lockfile, and
nothing removes it. A passing check means the inclusions
hold, not that the project is unchanged. Restoring the
prior state requires deleting the entries by hand or
discarding the changes under version control, which is
itself a small argument for making the repair on a branch.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

This exercise has no single correct answer, because the
times depend on the package, the machine, and the network.
What a good answer establishes is the mechanism, and it
should report both timings and name the package.

The expected result is that the snapshot install is
substantially faster. The explanation is that Posit
Package Manager serves a prebuilt binary for the declared
platform. Installing a binary is unpacking an archive;
installing from source is compiling it. For a package
carrying compiled code, typically anything depending on
`Rcpp`, the difference is commonly an order of magnitude
or more.

The instructive case is the one that does not show a large
difference. A pure-R package has little to compile, so the
two paths do similar work and the timings converge. A
reader who happens to pick such a package and reports a
small difference has the right finding, provided they
identify why. Two other conditions can flatten the
difference and are worth checking before concluding
anything. First, the `renv` cache may already hold the
package, in which case neither install does real work.
Second, PPM does not serve binaries for every platform,
so a machine whose platform is unserved falls back to
source in both arms.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

This exercise also has no single correct answer, since
what differs depends on the date chosen and on the size of
the dependency tree. A good answer reports the count of
differing packages, gives one or two concrete version
pairs, and draws the general conclusion.

The general conclusion is that `rang` reconstructs what
was *current on a date*, which is not the same thing as
what an analysis *actually used*. The two coincide only if
the original analyst installed everything on that date and
never updated anything afterward. That is not how most
projects proceed. Reconstruction by date is therefore an
approximation, and a lockfile is a record; the
approximation is what one falls back on when the record
does not exist.

The number of differing packages will generally grow with
the age of the date and with the depth of the dependency
tree, since a difference anywhere in the transitive
closure counts. A package whose version happens to be
unchanged is not evidence that the reconstruction
succeeded, only that that particular package was quiet
over the interval.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

A passing dependency check establishes that the triad
holds: every package the code uses is declared, and every
declared package is pinned in the lockfile. That is
exactly the L1 property, pinned packages, and the check is
the evidence for it.

It is not L2, because the lockfile pins packages and
nothing beneath them. The R version is recorded in the
lockfile but not supplied by it. The operating system, the
system libraries, the locale, the time zone, and the
numerical libraries are all outside its scope. L2 requires
an artifact that fixes the operating system, the R
runtime, and the system libraries, which is what
@sec-containers is about. Even L2 does not guarantee the
numerical libraries: an image determines which BLAS is
installed, but the thread count and the CPU still vary.

For a concrete unpinned determinant, the numerical-library
layer is the cleanest example of what a lockfile misses,
though no rung of the ladder fixes it completely. Two
machines can hold
identical pinned package sets and still link against
different BLAS implementations, reference BLAS on one and
Apple's Accelerate or Intel MKL on the other. Because
these reorder the floating-point summations inside a
matrix decomposition, a principal-components analysis or a
mixed-model fit can return results that agree to several
decimal places and differ in the last. A sign flip on a
component can make the difference visible in a plot. The
lockfile is silent on all of it, and setting a seed does
not help, because the difference is not stochastic.

A second acceptable answer names the locale. Two machines
under different collation orders sort character vectors
differently. This changes which row is taken first in a
tie and can therefore change a reported result through a
`slice()` or a `first()`, with no error raised anywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Exercise 8

`renv::init()` writes a generated `.gitignore` inside
`renv/`. Under `renv` 1.2.3's default settings it
excludes `library/`, `local/` (local package sources),
`cellar/`, `lock/`, `python/`, `sandbox/`, and `staging/`.
It leaves `renv/activate.R` and `renv/settings.json` to be
committed, along with the lockfile `renv.lock` at the
project root. The rule follows the same
line the version-control chapter draws between what must
be committed and what must never be. Here it is applied to
a different kind of large, regenerable, and
machine-specific content rather than to restricted data.

Committing `library/` would not merely waste space; it
would defeat the lockfile's purpose outright. `renv.lock`
exists to be a small, portable, human-readable
description from which the library can be
*rebuilt* on any machine. If the library itself were
committed, a collaborator on a different operating system
or architecture would receive compiled binaries built for
someone else's platform. Because their versions match the
lockfile, `renv::restore()` would likely treat them as
already installed, and a package with compiled code would
then fail when it loads. Moreover,
the repository would grow by orders of magnitude for
content that `renv::restore()` already knows how to
regenerate from the one file that actually matters.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-deps}

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `renv::init()` | Creates the project-local library and a first `renv.lock`. |
| `renv::snapshot()` | Scans the code for referenced packages and writes their installed versions to `renv.lock`. |
| `renv::restore()` | Reads `renv.lock` and reinstalls exactly the versions it records. |
| `renv::dependencies(files)` | Scans one or more files for the packages they name (`library()`, `::`, and similar), base packages included, without touching the lockfile. |
| `make check-renv` / `zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = TRUE)` | Checks and repairs the code-to-`DESCRIPTION`-to-lockfile triad. |
| `zzrenvcheck::check_packages(auto_fix = FALSE, strict = TRUE, error_on_fail = TRUE)` | The CI form: checks only, and fails the build on a violation. |
| `options(repos = c(CRAN = '.../cran/YYYY-MM-DD'))` | Points installs at a dated, fixed snapshot of the repository. |
| Rule of thumb | A lockfile pins the package layer and nothing beneath it; L1, not L2. |
| Rule of thumb | An oracle, a declared dependency, or a pinned version must come from outside the thing it checks; a lockfile is no exception for file integrity. |
| Habit 3 | Never let restricted data reach an unapproved model endpoint, even to ask a dependency question. |

## Further reading

The authoritative reference for the tool is @ushey2020,
the package documentation for `renv`. Its introductory
and collaboration vignettes are the fastest route to
fluent daily use, and its treatment of the cache and of
custom repositories repays study once the basics are in
hand. The glossary entry
[`renv` and `packrat`](glossary.qmd#gloss-renv-and-packrat)
summarizes the relationship of `renv` to its predecessor.

For the date-based alternatives, @chan2023 presents
`rang` and its strategy of reconstructing a historical
environment from CRAN's archive. It gives a clear account
of the cases where hindsight succeeds and where it cannot.
@simonsohn2026 documents `groundhog` and its run-time,
date-stamped loading model, and @capsule describes the
lazy discipline that `capsule` layers over `renv`.
Reading the three together clarifies that pinning the
package layer admits several idioms with different
demands on foresight.

On the discipline of where a package belongs, the
placement whitepaper accompanying the framework develops
the two-test decision procedure and the two-layer model
that this chapter summarizes. It is the place to turn
when a package sits awkwardly between the lockfile and
the Dockerfile. Finally, the boundary this chapter
insists on, that the lockfile pins the packages and
nothing beneath them, is taken up directly in
@sec-containers. There the container fixes the R version,
the operating system, and the system libraries that
`renv` by design does not.
